results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, for days 61 through 75 of your stay you'd pay **$434 per day**. Days 61–90: You pay $434 each day.

For context, Days 1–60: After you pay the $1,736 Part A deductible, you pay $0 each day. So for a 75-day stay in one benefit period, that works out to the **$1,736** deductible plus 15 days × $434 = **$6,510**, for a total of **$8,246**. Note that these amounts are listed as 2026 figures: Each time you start a new benefit period, you must pay $1,736 (in 2026) before Medicare starts to pay.

results.answer:
As a federal retiree with an OPM annuity who isn't entitled to Social Security or RRB benefits, you must ask to have your Part B premiums deducted from your annuity. Contact your local Social Security office to make your request. Visit SSA.gov/locator to find your local office.

If you don't set up the deduction, you'll get a bill for your Part B premium. Typically, Part B premiums are billed quarterly (every 3 months). There are 4 ways to pay your premium bill, including:
- Online through your secure Medicare account: Visit Medicare.gov/account to log into (or create) your Medicare account. Then, select "Pay my premium" to make a payment by credit card, debit card, Health Savings Account (HSA) card, or from your checking or savings account. This free service is the fastest way to pay your premium.
- Medicare Easy Pay: This free service automatically deducts your payment from your account (the excerpt cuts off here; the other payment methods aren't included in these documents).

results.answer:

Your out-of-pocket maximum is **$7,500**. For a Self Only enrollment, your out-of-pocket maximum for eligible coinsurance and copayment amounts is $7,500 when you use Preferred providers. Some caveats:
- Only eligible expenses for Preferred provider services count toward these limits.
- Certain types of expenses do not accumulate to the maximum, and you must continue to pay them even after you reach it.
- You must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care.

results.answer:

- Preferred facilities: **$250 copayment per day per facility**
- Member facilities: **$250 copayment per day per facility**
- Non-member facilities: **$250** copayment per day per facility, plus any difference between our allowance and the billed amount

Other charges may apply. You pay 35% of the Plan allowance for agents or drugs administered or obtained in connection with your care. This could include contrast used for the MRI. You may also be responsible for paying a higher copayment per day per facility if other diagnostic and/or treatment services are billed in addition to the services listed here.

results.answer:
Completing the Blue Health Assessment (BHA) gets you a personalized health plan and makes you eligible for health account dollars.

- **Health action plan:** Your BHA answers are evaluated to create a unique health action plan. Based on the results of your BHA, you can select personalized goals, receive supportive advice, and easily track your progress through our online coaching tool, Daily Habits.
- **Health account dollars:** We will add $40 to your health account for each goal achieved, up to a maximum of three goals per year. By completing the BHA and a maximum of three health goals, you can earn up to a total of $170 in health account dollars. The excerpts don't state the BHA's own reward separately. Since three goals at **$40** each equal $120, the BHA portion appears to be **$50**. You must complete the BHA and your selected goals during the calendar year in order to receive these incentives.
- **Free blood pressure monitor (if you have hypertension):** One eligibility criterion is that you complete the Blue Health Assessment (BHA), and indicate that you have been diagnosed with hypertension. The other is that at least one medical claim has been processed during the past 12 months with a reported diagnosis of hypertension.

This section applies to both Standard and Basic Option.

results.answer:
Under the Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan, you place your first mail order like this:

- Complete the initial mail order form
- Enclose your prescription and copayment
- Mail your order to CVS Caremark, P.O. Box 1590, Pittsburgh, PA 15230-1590

Instead of mailing it, your physician may call in your initial prescription at 800-262-7890, TTY: 711. You are responsible for the copayment.

For timing, allow up to two weeks for delivery on the first order. Refills are faster: allow up to ten days for delivery on refills. You can order refills by calling the same number or through www.fepblue.org.

There are a few things to check before you order:

- Who can use it: Standard Option members may use our Mail Service Prescription Drug Program. Under Basic Option, the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program is available only to members with primary Medicare Part B coverage.
- Prior approval: CVS Caremark, the program administrator, will hold your prescription for you up to 30 days while you get any required prior approval. If prior approval is not obtained within 30 days, your prescription will be unable to be filled.
- Specialty drugs: Specialty drugs will not be dispensed through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program.

results.question: If a doctor doesn't accept assignment, what's the most extra they can charge me above the Medicare-approved amount?

results.answer:
A doctor who doesn't accept assignment can charge you up to **15%** above the Medicare-approved amount. In many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge."

The BCBS FEHB brochure says the same thing another way: a physician who does not accept Medicare assignment may not bill you for more than 115% of the amount Medicare bases its payment on, called the "limiting charge." If your physician tries to collect more than allowed by law, ask the physician to reduce the charges. If the physician does not, report the physician to the Medicare carrier that sent you the MSN form.

Also note that you might have to pay the entire charge at the time of service.

Some Medigap policies cover care abroad: Some Medigap policies also cover services that Original Medicare doesn't cover, like medical care when you travel outside the U.S.

results.question: How do I appeal a decision about a claim under Original Medicare?

results.answer:
If you have Original Medicare, the appeal process works like this:

- Get the "Medicare Summary Notice" (MSN) that shows the item or service you're appealing.
- Circle the item(s) on the MSN you disagree with. Write an explanation of why you disagree with the decision. You can write on the MSN or on a separate piece of paper and attach it to the MSN.
- Include your name, phone number, and Medicare Number on the MSN. Keep a copy for your records.
- Send the MSN, or a copy, to the company that handles bills for Medicare (Medicare Administrative Contractor) listed on the MSN. You can include any information you have about your appeal, like information from your health care provider.

Alternatively, you can use Form CMS-20027. To get this form, visit Medicare.gov/basics/forms-publications-mailings/forms/appeals, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to have a copy mailed to you. TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

Deadlines and timing: You must file your appeal by the date in the MSN. If you missed the deadline for appealing, you may still file an appeal and get a decision if you can show good cause for missing the deadline. You'll generally get a decision from the Medicare Administrative Contractor within **60 days** after they get your request. If Medicare will cover the item(s) or service(s), it will be listed on your next MSN.

You can also ask your doctor, supplier, or other health care provider for any information to make your appeal stronger. Keep a copy of everything related to your appeal, including copies you send to Medicare or your plan. You can also get help filing an appeal from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

results.answer:
Yes, both sources describe a $35 limit on insulin, though they work differently.

**Medicare (Medicare & You 2027)**
- Plans can't charge you more than $35 for a one-month supply of each Part D-covered insulin you take, and you don't have to pay a deductible for insulin.
- Similar cost limits apply for traditional insulin used in Part B-covered insulin pumps.
- Your overall Part D out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,400 in 2027.

**2026 FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan**
- This is a fixed copayment rather than a stated cap. For Tier 2 (preferred insulins): $35 copayment for each purchase of up to a 30-day supply ($65 copayment for a 31 to 90-day supply) (no deductible). The page layout suggests this figure falls under the Standard Option column at network retail pharmacies, but the excerpt doesn't state that clearly.
- For Standard Option, Non-preferred retail pharmacies: You pay all charges.

results.question: What's the yearly Part B deductible in 2026, and which Medigap plans pay it?

results.answer:
The yearly Part B deductible is **$283 in 2026**. Under Original Medicare, if the Part B deductible applies, you must pay all costs (up to the Medicare-approved amount) until you meet the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).

The excerpts don't clearly show which Medigap plans pay it. The chart's "Medicare Part B deductible" row lists four entries (100% | 100% | 100%** 100%**), but the extracted text has lost the column alignment, so you can't tell which plan letters those entries belong to. The chart covers plans A | B | C | D | F* | G* | K | L | M | N, and if a box is empty, it means that service isn't covered by that Medigap plan and you're responsible for paying the cost.

Related notes from the same page:
- Plans K and L pay 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year after you meet your out-of-pocket yearly limit and your yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026). The out-of-pocket limit for Plan K is $8,000 and Plan L is $4,000 in 2026.
- You can't buy Medigap Plans C or F if you became eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.

To confirm which plans cover the deductible, check the original chart on page 80 or visit Medicare.gov for the latest amounts.

results.answer:
Generally, no. Under Basic Option you must use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. There are no benefits for care performed by Participating and Non-participating providers.

There are exceptions:

- **Emergencies and other listed circumstances:** You must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care. See Section 3 for exceptions under What you must do to get covered care.
- **Overseas care:** The Basic Option requirement to use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits does not apply when you receive overseas care.
- **If you have Medicare:** The Medicare section repeats the rule. Under Basic Option, you must see Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. See Section 3 for the exceptions to this requirement.
